title: Make Your Own Compost for Healthy Soil
excerpt: Use farm waste, dry leaves, grass, and manure to improve soil naturally.
keyPoints: Start with materials already on your farm.
The pile should be damp, not soaked.
Use compost when it is dark, crumbly, and smells earthy.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Compost helps improve soil, hold moisture, and feed crops slowly. You can start with materials already on your farm.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: Dry leaves or dry grass, crop waste, vegetable scraps, a small amount of animal manure, water, and a shaded, well-drained place.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Choose a shaded, well-drained place. Put dry materials at the bottom. Add green materials like crop waste or vegetable scraps. Add a small layer of manure or old compost. Sprinkle water so the pile is damp, not soaked. Cover with dry grass, leaves, or a sack. Turn the pile every 1-2 weeks. Use it when it is dark, crumbly, and smells earthy.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not add plastic. Do not add meat or oil. Do not use human waste. Do not add chemical containers. Avoid fresh diseased crop material.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate what compost materials are available on your farm and what crop you want to plant.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Start a small compost pile this week using materials already on your farm.

title: How to Mulch Your Farm and Save Water
excerpt: Use dry grass, leaves, or crop residue to keep soil cool and reduce water loss.
keyPoints: Mulch helps soil stay cooler.
Keep mulch away from the plant stem.
Use clean dry grass, leaves, or crop residue.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Mulching covers the soil with dry grass, leaves, or crop residue. It helps reduce water loss, protects soil from heat, and can reduce weeds.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: Dry grass, dry leaves, rice straw, maize stalk pieces, or clean crop residue. Avoid materials with fresh disease signs or weed seeds.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Water the crop first if the soil is dry. Spread mulch around the crop in a thin layer. Leave a small space around the stem. Add more mulch when it breaks down. Check under the mulch for pests during weekly field checks.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not pile mulch tightly against stems. Do not use plastic waste. Do not use diseased crop leaves. Do not make the layer so thick that water cannot enter.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate which mulch materials are safest for your crop and season.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Mulch one small crop bed this week and compare soil moisture after two days.

title: How to Use Poultry Manure Safely
excerpt: Learn why fresh manure can burn crops and how to use it more safely.
keyPoints: Fresh poultry manure can burn crops.
Compost or age manure before use.
Keep manure away from edible leaves and fruits.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Poultry manure can feed soil, but fresh manure is strong. If used wrongly, it can burn crops, smell badly, or contaminate produce.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: Dry poultry manure, dry leaves or grass, a compost corner, water, and time for the manure to age before planting.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Mix poultry manure with dry plant material. Keep it in a compost pile or covered place. Let it break down before applying. Use small amounts. Apply to soil, not directly on edible leaves or fruits.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not put fresh poultry manure directly on young roots. Do not spread manure on leafy vegetables close to harvest. Do not store manure where rain can wash it into water sources.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate how to use manure for your crop, soil condition, and planting time.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Start aging or composting poultry manure before using it on young crops.

title: Crop Rotation: Why Maize Should Not Stand Alone Every Season
excerpt: Simple crop rotation ideas to protect soil and reduce pest pressure.
keyPoints: Repeating one crop can weaken soil.
Rotation can reduce some pest pressure.
Legumes can help improve soil.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Planting maize on the same plot every season can reduce soil strength and allow some pests or diseases to build up. Rotation gives the soil a break.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A simple record of what you planted last season, available seed, land space, and a crop that fits your market or household needs.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Write down last season's crop. Choose a different crop family when possible. Add legumes where they fit. Keep crop residue managed well. Watch the new crop closely for early pest signs.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not rotate without checking market or food needs. Do not move from one stressed crop to another without improving soil. Do not ignore drainage and spacing.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate what crop you grew last season and what options fit your region and season.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Write down what was planted on each plot last season before choosing the next crop.

title: Before You Spray: 3 Things to Check First
excerpt: Check weather, wind, and the real crop problem before spraying.
keyPoints: Check rain before spraying.
Avoid strong wind.
Confirm the real problem first.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Spraying at the wrong time can waste money and may not solve the crop problem. Check the weather, wind, and visible signs first.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A weather check, a quick wind check, a close look under leaves, and a clear reason for spraying.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Check if rain is expected. Check if the wind is strong. Inspect the crop closely. Confirm whether you see pests, disease signs, nutrient stress, or water stress. Follow label instructions only when spraying is truly needed.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not spray before rain. Do not spray in strong wind. Do not spray just because leaves look weak. Do not mix products without trusted advice.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate: Can I spray today? Use Crop Doctor if a photo would help confirm what you see.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Check rain and wind before mixing any spray.

title: Weekly Crop Field Check
excerpt: A simple weekly routine for checking leaves, pests, wilting, and plant growth.
keyPoints: Check bottom leaves first.
Look under leaves for pests.
Compare weak plants with healthy plants.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: A weekly field check helps you catch crop problems early. Walk the field slowly and compare affected plants with healthy ones.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A notebook or phone, time to inspect several plants, and good light so you can see leaves clearly.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Check bottom leaves. Look under leaves. Check stems and new growth. Look for wilting, yellowing, spots, holes, or insects. Note where the problem appears in the field.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not check only one plant. Do not ignore lower leaves. Do not spray before you know what problem you are trying to solve.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate what you see, which crop is affected, and whether symptoms are on old leaves, new leaves, or the whole plant.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Inspect five plants today and write down the first symptom you see.

title: Rainy Season Farm Checklist
excerpt: Prepare drainage, seed, tools, and labour before heavy rains.
keyPoints: Clear drainage paths early.
Keep seed dry.
Avoid planting in waterlogged soil.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Heavy rain can delay planting, damage young crops, and spread some crop problems. Preparing early makes field work easier.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: Clear drains, dry seed storage, working tools, labour plans, and a simple weather check before major field work.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Clear drainage paths. Check seed and tools early. Plan labour before the field gets busy. Avoid planting in waterlogged soil. Check rain before spraying or harvesting.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not wait until the field is flooded. Do not store seed where it can get wet. Do not apply fertilizer or spray before heavy rain.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate whether rain may affect planting, spraying, harvesting, or irrigation decisions.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Walk the field and clear the main drainage path today.

title: Simple Raised Beds for Vegetables
excerpt: Use raised beds to improve drainage and protect vegetable roots.
keyPoints: Raised beds help water drain away.
Beds make crop rows easier to manage.
Mulch can help raised beds hold moisture.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Raised beds lift vegetable roots above standing water. They are useful where rain or irrigation leaves the soil too wet.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A hoe, prepared soil, compost if available, and enough space between beds for walking and drainage.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Mark the bed area. Loosen the soil. Add compost if available. Raise the bed above the path. Smooth the top. Leave drainage space between beds. Mulch after planting where suitable.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not make beds where water cannot escape. Do not make paths too narrow. Do not plant too close together.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate about spacing, watering, and whether raised beds suit your crop and season.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Prepare one small raised bed before expanding to the full garden.

title: How to Prepare Produce Before Selling
excerpt: Sort, pack, estimate quantity, and prepare buyer details.
keyPoints: Sort damaged produce first.
Estimate quantity clearly.
Prepare pickup or delivery details.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Good harvest preparation helps buyers understand quality, quantity, timing, and pickup needs. It reduces confusion before sale.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: Clean containers, sorting space, quantity estimates, produce photos if needed, harvest date, and pickup or delivery details.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Remove damaged produce. Group similar sizes together. Count or weigh clearly. Prepare packaging. Write down location, quantity, harvest date, and contact details.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not mix damaged produce with good produce. Do not guess quantity. Do not promise delivery before checking transport.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate if you notice crop quality problems before harvest or need a checklist before selling.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Sort your harvest and write down quantity, location, and preferred pickup time.

title: How to Sort and Pack Vegetables for Buyers
excerpt: Simple steps to make produce cleaner, easier to count, and more buyer-ready.
keyPoints: Separate damaged produce.
Use clean crates or sacks.
Keep quantity easy to confirm.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Sorting and packing helps buyers trust what they are receiving. Clean, counted produce is easier to inspect and transport.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A clean sorting area, crates or sacks, shade, water for cleaning only where appropriate, and a simple way to count or estimate quantity.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Sort out damaged produce. Group by size or quality. Keep produce shaded. Pack in clean containers. Count crates, sacks, bunches, or kilograms clearly.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not pack wet produce tightly if it may spoil. Do not hide damaged produce inside good produce. Do not overfill containers.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate for a harvest preparation checklist before contacting buyers.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Prepare one clean sorting area before harvest day.

title: How to Use GG FarmMate
excerpt: Ask better questions, use live tools, and get practical next steps.
keyPoints: Ask one clear question at a time.
Mention crop, symptom, and recent weather.
Follow the next step before adding more details.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: GG FarmMate is the live daily farming companion for practical farm questions, crop photos, crop timing, planting support, and daily farm guidance.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A clear question, the crop name, what you can see, and any recent rain, watering, spraying, or field change.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Open GG FarmMate. Ask one farming question. Answer follow-up questions if FarmMate asks. Use Crop Doctor when a photo can reduce guessing.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not ask many unrelated questions at once. Do not leave out the crop name. Do not treat FarmMate as a replacement for an extension officer during serious outbreaks.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate when you need one practical next step for planting, spraying, crop symptoms, watering, harvest preparation, or tool guidance.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Open GG FarmMate and ask one clear question about your farm today.

title: How to Use Crop Doctor
excerpt: Upload a clear crop photo so FarmMate can avoid guessing.
keyPoints: Use good light.
Show the affected crop part clearly.
Use the result as guidance, not a final diagnosis.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: Crop Doctor uses a crop photo to guide checks. It can help reduce guessing, but it does not replace local expert confirmation for serious problems.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A clear photo of the affected leaf, stem, fruit, or whole plant. Good daylight helps FarmMate see visible signs.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Take a clear photo. Upload it to Crop Doctor. Read the visible signs, possible issue, recommended action, prevention, and next best action.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not upload blurry photos. Do not crop out the affected part. Do not treat the result as guaranteed. Do not apply chemicals before checking the real problem.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate about the Crop Doctor result when you need help deciding what to check next.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Upload one clear crop photo when you see a visible crop problem.

title: Video Guide: How to Use Crop Doctor
excerpt: A short lesson for farmers learning how to upload crop photos for advisory guidance.
keyPoints: Take a clear photo.
Use Crop Doctor for visible crop problems.
Ask FarmMate what to check next.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body: This short lesson supports Crop Doctor practice. The video card shows Coming soon until the training video is live.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.body: A phone camera, good light, and a visible crop problem to photograph.

sections.heading: Steps
sections.body: Open Crop Doctor, upload a clear photo, read the result, and use Ask FarmMate if you need help with the next check.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid
sections.body: Do not upload unclear photos or assume the result is a guaranteed diagnosis.

sections.heading: When to ask FarmMate
sections.body: Ask FarmMate if the Crop Doctor result is uncertain or if you need help choosing the next field check.

sections.heading: Next action
sections.body: Open Crop Doctor when you have a clear crop photo.
